transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-07-02
Time: 15:00 PDT
Duration reported: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Dmitri (Redwood SE), Laura (CTO - OrionTech), Ben (Head of Infra), Priya (Security), Sam (Procurement)

[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate your time. Quick intro - I'm Maya, account exec on the infra team, and Dmitri is our solutions engineer.
[00:07] Dmitri (Redwood): Hi all, excited to dig in. We know OrionTech is evaluating Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private so we'll focus on dedicated capacity details today.
[00:14] Laura (OrionTech): Thanks. High level - we're building a customer-facing summarization product that needs stable inference latency and isolation. We've been testing Hosted but want reserved GPUs for predictable throughput and to meet compliance.
[00:26] Ben (OrionTech): Yeah, also want the ability to burst to hosted when demand spikes, we don't want to overcommit monthly.
[00:33] Priya (OrionTech): From security side, SOC2 and KMS integration are musts, plus audit logs and SSO. We're regulated so data residency matters too.
[00:42] Maya (Redwood): Totally. Quick question on scale - what's your expected steady-state and peak? Concurrency, request size, typical sequence lengths?
[00:50] Ben: For steady state about 200 concurrent sessions, peaks up to 800 for 30-60 minutes during business hours. Typical requests are 512 tokens, occasionally up to 2k. Latency target is p95 under 300ms for our user flows, p99 under 750ms ideally.
[01:12] Dmitri: Helpful. For those numbers we usually size dedicated pools by GPU type and concurrency - e.g., 8 A100-ish equivalents for that pattern, but exact numbers depend on model type, quantization, and batching. What models are you running?
[01:27] Laura: We're using a mix - a fine-tuned open LLM for summarization (7B-ish) and a larger 13B for more complex docs. We're exploring quantization but need to validate quality.
[01:39] Dmitri: That maps well. With quantized 7B and 13B variants, you can get decent throughput and lower cost. Redwood Dedicated supports pinned model versions and we can do automatic fallback to hosted variants if the dedicated pool is saturated.
[01:53] Sam (Procurement): Can you explain burst behavior - is that seamless? Does data flow through Hosted when bursting? That's a compliance question.
[02:02] Maya: Good callout. Burst can be configured two ways: route to Redwood Hosted (managed) or to a separate burst pool in a different dedicated cluster. If you use Hosted for burst, we have options for data handling - you can opt for no logging or ephemeral handling, but some customers prefer a private burst pool to avoid external egress.
[02:20] Priya: Hosted routing is a red flag for us unless we can guarantee encryption + no retention. Do you support customer-managed KMS for Hosted bursts?
[02:28] Dmitri: For Redwood Hosted, you can enable customer KMS (bring-your-own) for at-rest encryption and restrict logs. We can also configure that requests routed to Hosted for burst are not retained for training and are covered under the same contractual terms. We'll include the SOC2 + data handling language in the docs.
[02:43] Ben: What's the typical cold-start / scale time for dedicated pools - say we autoscale from 8 to 20 GPUs during a spike?
[02:51] Dmitri: Autoscaling times vary by instance type and region; warm scaling within a dedicated pool (activating reserved nodes) is a matter of seconds to a couple minutes if nodes are pre-warmed. Cold provisioning new GPUs can be 5-15 minutes depending on infra. That's why we recommend a small buffer and a burst-to-hosted fallback for very short spikes.
[03:12] Laura: Ok that makes sense. We want predictable per-token costs too. How do you handle cost visibility with dedicated?
[03:20] Maya: Dedicated is billed as a reserved capacity contract (monthly). We provide token/throughput analytics in Redwood Console so you can see per-route and per-model cost breakdowns, plus token-level latency. Batching and KV caching can reduce unit cost - Dmitri can share best-practice batch sizes for your models.
[03:36] Dmitri: For your 512-2k sequences, continuous KV cache helps a lot if you have repeated context. Batching improves throughput but increases latency for single-shot requests; we can tune to your p95 targets.
[03:49] Ben: Are there constraints around KV cache when bursting to Hosted? Do those keys migrate?
[03:56] Dmitri: KV cache is per-runtime. If you fall back to hosted, you won't have the dedicated node's in-memory KV cache. You can mitigate with prefix caching at the application level or use sticky routing for sessions. It's a tradeoff.
[04:12] Priya: On the security side - SSO/SAML integration, SCIM, RBAC, audit logs - do you provide those for Dedicated and Private?
[04:20] Maya: Yes, Dedicated clusters can integrate with your SSO via SAML/SCIM, and we support RBAC at the route and project level. Audit logs and network flow logs are available; for Private we can ship logs to your SIEM. We'll attach sample RBAC policies.
[04:35] Priya: KMS - do you support HSM or customer-managed keys?
[04:39] Dmitri: We support customer-managed keys (BYOK) via common KMS providers, and for Private deployments we can integrate with HSMs. We'll include HSM notes in the security packet.
[04:50] Laura: Another concern is vendor lock-in. If we commit to reserved capacity, can we export model weights or run an on-prem package later?
[04:59] Maya: We support Private deployments and can help with migration paths. Models themselves are customer-managed; you keep the weights and can run on-prem or in a VPC. Redwood's value is in the runtime and orchestration, but we try to make migration feasible.
[05:12] Ben: For SLAs - what uptime and latency SLAs exist for Dedicated?
[05:18] Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets for committed pools. Exact numbers vary by contract tier - we'll include example SLA terms in the pricing docs.
[05:27] Sam: On procurement, what's the minimum commitment and payment cadence?
[05:31] Maya: Typical is monthly or annual reserved commitments. Minimums depend on GPU type; we'll include multiple commit tiers. We can also do a pilot month at a smaller commit to validate.
[05:42] Ben: For benchmarks - we'd like Redwood to run our workload and show p95/p99 and throughput. Can you run distributed benchmarking?
[05:49] Dmitri: Yes - we can run a benchmark with your workload, feed in sample prompts, sequences, and concurrency. We'll test both quantized and FP32 variants, and show latency breakdowns, token throughput, and cost estimates.
[06:04] Laura: Great. One operational question - who manages OS/driver updates and kernel compatibility for dedicated GPUs?
[06:11] Dmitri: Redwood manages the serving runtime and coordinates driver updates; for Dedicated we handle runtime updates and kernel selection, but we coordinate maintenance windows with customers. For Private on-prem, the customer handles physical host updates unless we have a managed option.
[06:27] Maya: I'm going to recap quickly - we heard: steady 200 concurrent, peaks to 800, sequence 512-2k, p95 under ~300ms target, need SOC2, KMS, SSO, and a bursting strategy to either Hosted or a private burst pool. Next steps: pricing, security docs, and a benchmark. Any other blockers?
[06:45] Priya: Please include data residency language - we have EU-hosted customers and need logs stored in-region.
[06:50] Dmitri: Noted - we have regional options and can pin clusters to regions. We'll include region/residency config.
[06:58] Sam: Budget-wise we need a formal quote for procurement - include payment terms and cancellation policy.
[07:04] Maya: We'll include all that.
[07:08] Laura: Timing - we aim to choose a vendor by end of month; we'll need a pilot next week to validate.
[07:14] Maya: We should be able to run a pilot/benchmark the week of 2026-07-06.
[07:18] Ben: Sounds good.
[07:20] Maya: Okay thanks everyone - we'll follow up with the docs and set up the benchmark cadence.
[07:24] Dmitri: I'll attach the SOC2 and network diagrams and propose config options for 8/16/24 GPU pools.
[07:31] Laura: Thanks, talk soon.
